newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egyptian state moves in on Alexandria refinery.
newsitem.headline: Egyptian state moves in on Alexandria refinery.

text.p: The Egyptian public sector has quadrupled its capital in a $1.2 billion joint-venture to build an oil refinery with Israelis in a structural change which also doubles the capital of the company, executives said on Wednesday.

The change gives the state's Egyptian General Petroleum Corporation (EGPC) effective control of the project, Middle East Oil Refinery (MIDOR), which was initially dominated by the Merhaf Group of Israel and Swiss-based Maska Swiss, led by Egyptian businessman Hussein Salem.
Salem, who remains chairman of MIDOR, told Reuters on Wednesday that EGPC now has 40 percent of the capital, which has risen to $360 million from $180 million.

The Egyptian companies Petrojet and Enppi (Engineering Petroleum and Process Industries) have taken 10 percent each, he added. The companies nominally have private-sector status but EGPC is the biggest shareholder in both.
Merhaf and Maska Swiss did not contribute to the capital increase so their stakes have halved to 20 percent each. They originally had 40 percent each, with 20 percent for EGPC.

When it began, the project attracted much attention because of the Israeli stake and because it was then the biggest private-sector investment in downstream oil activities in Egypt, where all other refineries are state-owned.
To reflect the change in shareholdings, the Egyptian state has appointed Sameh Fahmy as president, vice-chairman and managing director of MIDOR. Fahmy was previously EGPC vice-chairman for projects.
Salem said the structural change took place last month with the full approval of all the parties. "The aim is to upgrade the financing," he added, without elaboration.
Salem said MIDOR would not need to borrow much to set up the refinery in the Mediterranean city of Alexandria but he declined to go into the company's financing plans.
MIDOR has said that the European Investment Bank is extending long-term credit of $300 million and that several export credit agencies have expressed an interest in financing.
"The project is going ahead just fine. We are on target for the refinery to open by the end of the year 2000," Salem added.

The plan is to process 100,000 barrels of crude a day, mostly into unleaded petrol. MIDOR said in July that Israel and Egypt would each get a third of production while the rest went to adjacent markets such as Turkey, southern Italy, Greece, Cyprus and the Palestinian territories.

Under contracts signed last year, Technipetrol of Italy and Technip of France will build the refinery. The U.S. companies UOP, Conoco and Bechtel will supply technology and Louisiana Carbon will participate in product offtakes.
